name: Cassiopeia
introduction: is the vain queen of Greek myth, easy to find as a bright W or M of five stars lying in the Milky Way, opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris. From most of Europe, North America and northern Asia, she never sets; according to legend, she was condemned to circle the pole, spending half of each night upside down.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Cassiopeia changed how people understood the heavens. In November 1572, a new star blazed here, outshining Venus for a time. Tycho Brahe’s careful measurements showed that it did not move against the background stars, so it had to be far beyond the Moon. That observation challenged the ancient belief that the starry sky was perfect and unchanging. Today, we know it was a supernova.

A second, younger supernova remnant lies here as well. Light from the explosion that created Cassiopeia A reached Earth around 1680 without being clearly recorded. Its expanding debris, about 11,000 light-years away, is one of the brightest radio sources in the sky.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Schedar](hip:3179) is an orange giant about 230 light-years away. [Caph](hip:746), at the western end of the W, is much closer at 55 light-years and pulsates slightly several times a day.

The central star, [Tiansi](hip:4427) (Gamma Cassiopeiae), is a rapidly spinning hot star that sheds a disk of gas from its equator. Its brightness changes unpredictably, and it gives its name to a whole class of such stars. It also emits unexpectedly strong X-rays, which astronomers are still trying to explain. [Ruchbah](hip:6686) is an eclipsing binary that dims when its partner passes in front of it, and [Segin](hip:8886) completes the W.
Not far from the W lies the yellow dwarf [Achird](id:cns5-0239) (Eta Cassiopeiae), only about 19 light-years away and similar to the Sun.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Because Cassiopeia lies in the Milky Way, it is rich in star clusters and nebulae: the open clusters M52 and M103, NGC 457, nicknamed the Owl or E.T. Cluster, and the Heart and Soul Nebulae on the border with Perseus. In the other direction, the small galaxies NGC 147 and NGC 185 are satellites of the Andromeda Galaxy.
